material_units.source_text: (a) For $t\in[k\Delta t,(k+1)\Delta t]$ write $t=k\Delta t+\rho\Delta t$ with $\rho\in[0,1]$. Assumption 2.4 gives $\|x(t)-x(k\Delta t)\|\le\Xi$. Lipschitz continuity of $g_i(a_s,\cdot)$ with constant $L_x$ gives $|g_i(a_s,x(k\Delta t))-g_i(a_s,x(t))|\le L_x\|x(k\Delta t)-x(t)\|\le L_x\Xi$, hence $g_i(a_s,x(t))\ge g_i(a_s,x(k\Delta t))-L_x\Xi$. If the right-hand side is $\ge0$, then $\bar g_i(x(t))\ge g_i(a_s,x(t))\ge0$ because $x(t)$ is on the trajectory that starts at $x(t)$ under $a_s$ (Assumption 2.5). This is Lemma A.2.

material_units.source_text: So the backup that certified the previous sample is still safe at the trigger sample, which is what eq. 12 exploits. Without the $+\Xi$, passing the test at $k^*-1$ would only give $g_i(a_s,x(k^*))\ge-L_x\|x(k^*)-x(k^*-1)\|\ge-L_x\Xi$, which can be negative: the system could already be past the point of no return when the failure is detected, and moreover the states between the two samples would be uncovered. The condition must be one sampling interval ahead of the system.
